parts.title: Joining a cycling club
parts.intro: Part 1. You will hear a telephone conversation between a man who works for a cycling club and a woman who wants to join.

lines: GRAHAM: Good morning, Northgate Cycling Club, Graham speaking.
LENA: Oh, hello. I saw your poster in the sports centre, and I'd like to find out about joining the club.
GRAHAM: Of course. Can I take your name first, so I can send you some information?
LENA: Yes, it's Lena Durrant.
GRAHAM: Could you spell your surname for me?
LENA: Sure. It's D-U-double R-A-N-T.
GRAHAM: Thanks. And are you working, or studying at the moment? We have different types of membership.
LENA: I'm a student at the college. I'm doing a nursing course.
GRAHAM: Then you'd be able to have student membership. Full adult membership is sixty-five pounds a year, but for students it's forty-five.
LENA: That's reasonable. Does that include insurance?
GRAHAM: Yes, insurance is included for all members.
LENA: And is it possible to pay monthly? Money's a bit tight at the moment.
GRAHAM: I'm afraid not. It's one payment for the whole year, but you can pay online, or by card at one of our meetings.
LENA: OK, that's fine. And where do the rides start from? Someone told me you meet at the station.
GRAHAM: We used to, but the station car park is being rebuilt, so all the weekend rides now leave from the library car park, on Mill Road.
LENA: OK. I've only just started cycling again. Is there anything for beginners?
GRAHAM: Yes, there's a beginners' group. They used to meet on Tuesday evenings, but a lot of people found that difficult, so now they go out on Thursdays, at half past six.
LENA: Thursday would suit me better anyway. I have lectures until five on Tuesdays.
GRAHAM: Then that works well. The beginners' rides last about two hours, so you'd be back before nine.
LENA: Do I need any special equipment?

GRAHAM: Not really. A normal bike in good condition is fine, and you don't need special clothes, although a waterproof jacket is a good idea. The only thing we insist on is that everyone wears a helmet. If you haven't got lights, we can lend you some for the evening rides.
LENA: Is there a minimum age? My younger brother might want to come too. He's fifteen.
GRAHAM: Riders under sixteen are welcome, but they have to come with a parent or another adult member. So if you're with him, that's no problem.
LENA: That's good to know. How far do the beginners usually go?
GRAHAM: The experienced groups do around sixty kilometres, but the beginners' rides are much shorter. They're about twenty kilometres, on quiet roads.
LENA: That sounds manageable. Do you stop anywhere during the ride?
GRAHAM: Yes, there's always a break halfway. Some groups stop at a pub, but the beginners usually have tea at a farm just outside the town. It has a little café, and the cakes are very good.
LENA: Lovely. And what happens if the weather's bad?
GRAHAM: We go out in most weather, to be honest. But if it's really stormy, the ride leader sends everyone a text message by eight in the morning to say the ride is cancelled.
LENA: Right. Is there any training for new riders? I'm a bit nervous about riding in traffic.
GRAHAM: We run a road safety course once a month. It's normally twenty pounds, but members only pay twelve.
LENA: I'd definitely like to do that. How do I sign up?
GRAHAM: You can join online, or come along to our monthly meeting. That's on the first Monday of the month, in the room above the bike shop on Station Street.
LENA: The first Monday. I'll try to come to the next one. Thanks very much for your help.
GRAHAM: You're welcome. See you there.

parts.title: Volunteering at a science museum
parts.intro: Part 2. You will hear a woman talking to a group of new volunteers at a science museum.

lines: MARIA: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Harbourside Science Museum. I'm Maria, and I coordinate our volunteer programme. Before we walk around the building, I'd like to tell you a little about the museum and what we'll be asking you to do.
MARIA: The museum opened in 1987, and last year we welcomed just over three hundred thousand visitors, which is a record for us. About a third of those were school pupils.

MARIA: Many visitors assume this building was once a railway station, probably because of the clock tower. In fact, it was built as a warehouse for the shipping companies. The fish market, which people also mention, was next door, where the car park is now.

MARIA: Now, what will you be doing? We do have volunteers in the shop, and a few who guide adult tour groups, but the main reason we need you is the school groups. We have up to six classes a day, and they all take part in hands-on activities, which our volunteers run.

MARIA: Each shift lasts four hours, either in the morning or the afternoon, and we ask you to do at least two shifts a month. You'll be given a green T-shirt and a name badge, which you collect from the staff room on your first day.

MARIA: Some of you have asked about training. We used to have an online course, but we found that people preferred to learn on the job, so we stopped it. The two-day training course you may have heard about is for paid staff only. What we ask is that you spend your first three shifts working alongside one of our experienced volunteers.

MARIA: And a word about benefits. I'm afraid we can't offer free parking, as the car park belongs to the council. But you'll get a twenty per cent discount in the café, which is very popular. Family tickets aren't included, although we do hold a free family evening for volunteers twice a year.
MARIA: Now let me give you a quick overview of the galleries. On the ground floor, the Ocean Gallery has just reopened after a year of renovation, so it's looking wonderful.
MARIA: Above it, the Flight Hall is where you'll find our most popular exhibit: the full-size glider hanging from the ceiling. Almost every visitor wants a photograph with it.
MARIA: In the Energy Room, one of our scientists gives a live demonstration twice a day, at eleven and three. It's usually something with electricity, and it can be quite loud.
MARIA: The Weather Lab is quite small, so visitors need to reserve a time slot when they buy their ticket.
MARIA: People sometimes think you need to book for the Space Dome, but you don't. Just remember that it's closed every Monday, when the projector is cleaned and checked.
MARIA: And finally, outside, there's the Discovery Garden. It's designed for our youngest visitors. Children under five love the sand and water area, and parents can sit in the shade.

MARIA: One more practical point before we set off. The museum is open from ten until six, but volunteers should arrive by half past nine so that everything is ready before the first school group comes in. Lunch breaks are taken in the staff room, not in the galleries.
MARIA: Right, let's start the tour.

parts.title: Planning a research report
parts.intro: Part 3. You will hear two students, Kai and Rosa, discussing their research project with their tutor, Dr Ellis.

lines: DR ELLIS: Come in, both of you. So, how's the project on plastic waste in the university canteen going?
ROSA: Quite well, I think. We've finished the student survey, but we had a few problems with it.
DR ELLIS: Before we get to that, remind me how you sent it out.
KAI: We put a link on the student union website and on the canteen notice board, and we left it open for two weeks.
DR ELLIS: And what kind of problems did you have?
KAI: Well, the main one was that we only got sixty-three responses, which is much fewer than we'd hoped for.
ROSA: And some of the questions were confusing. Several people said they didn't understand what we meant by single-use packaging, so their answers weren't very useful.
DR ELLIS: Was the survey too long? That's a common problem.
KAI: No, people seemed to finish it quite quickly. And we were worried that only students who care about the environment would answer, but actually we got a good mix.
DR ELLIS: Good. So what are you going to change for the second round?
ROSA: We're going to add a short definition at the start, so everyone understands the key terms. We thought about offering a prize to get more responses, but the department doesn't allow that.

KAI: So instead we'll ask lecturers to give students five minutes at the end of a class to fill it in. We'll also do some short interviews with the canteen staff, because they see what people actually throw away.
DR ELLIS: Both sensible. Are you keeping it online?
ROSA: Yes, a paper version would take too long to process.
DR ELLIS: And when are you planning to run it?
KAI: Straight after the mid-term break. That gives us three weeks to collect the responses before we start writing up the results.
DR ELLIS: That's a little tight, but it should be possible if you start analysing the data while the survey is still open.

DR ELLIS: Now, I've read the draft of your report. Overall, it's a promising start, and the topic is one the canteen managers are genuinely interested in, so it could have a real impact. Let me go through it section by section. Your introduction is fine, but it's far too long. You could say the same thing in half the space.
KAI: OK, we'll cut it down.
DR ELLIS: The literature review is interesting, but you haven't said where some of the figures come from. Every statistic needs a source.
ROSA: Right. We'll add the references.
DR ELLIS: Your methods section is very clearly organised. I could follow exactly what you did, step by step. Don't change it.
KAI: That's good to hear.
DR ELLIS: In the results section, you describe all the numbers in words. It would be much easier for the reader if you put them in a chart.
ROSA: Yes, we can do that.
DR ELLIS: The discussion is the weakest part at the moment. You say that students want less plastic, but you don't explain why, or what that means for the canteen. It needs more detail.
KAI: That's fair. We were running out of time when we wrote it.
DR ELLIS: And finally, the recommendations. They're good, but they belong at the end of the discussion rather than in a separate section. Move them there and the report will flow better.
ROSA: Thanks. That's really helpful. When would you like the next draft?
DR ELLIS: Let's say two weeks from today. And send me the new survey questions before you put them online, so I can check the wording.
KAI: We'll do that by Friday.

parts.title: Green roofs and urban heat
parts.intro: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about green roofs in cities.

lines: LECTURER: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at one response to a growing problem in cities: the urban heat island effect. In many large cities, temperatures are several degrees higher than in the surrounding countryside, especially at night.

LECTURER: The main cause is the materials we build with. Concrete and brick absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after dark, and asphalt, which is used for roads, absorbs the most heat of all. Cities also have fewer plants, so there is less cooling from evaporation, as water escapes from leaves.

LECTURER: This matters for more than comfort. During heatwaves, hospital admissions rise, and the people most at risk are the elderly and those with heart and lung conditions. Higher night-time temperatures are particularly dangerous, because the body has no chance to recover.

LECTURER: Green roofs are not a new idea. In parts of Scandinavia, houses have been built with grass roofs for centuries, mainly to keep the heat in during the winter. What is new is their use in modern cities to keep buildings cool.

LECTURER: One solution, then, is the green roof: a roof covered with a layer of growing plants. There are two main types. Intensive green roofs are like rooftop gardens, with deep soil, trees and paths. They are heavy and expensive, and the building usually has to be strengthened. Extensive green roofs are much lighter. They have a thin layer of soil, often just ten centimetres, and they are planted with tough, low-growing species such as sedum, which can survive long periods without rain.

LECTURER: So what are the benefits? The most obvious is temperature. Research in several cities has found that the surface of a green roof on a summer afternoon can be thirty degrees cooler than a conventional black roof. This also reduces the energy needed for air conditioning in the rooms below. The effect is greatest on the top floor; on lower floors, the difference is much smaller.

LECTURER: A second benefit concerns water. During heavy storms, drains in cities can become overloaded and cause flooding. A green roof holds a large part of the rainfall and releases it gradually, which takes pressure off the drainage system.

LECTURER: Green roofs also provide a habitat for wildlife. Studies have recorded many species of insects on them, including bees, which are important for pollination. And there is a less obvious economic benefit: the plants protect the waterproof layer underneath from sunlight, so the roof may last up to twice as long before it needs replacing.

LECTURER: However, there are limitations. The cost of installation is still a barrier for many building owners, although some city governments now offer grants. Maintenance is often underestimated: even extensive roofs need to be checked regularly for weeds and blocked drains. And in hot, dry climates, the plants may need watering, which reduces the environmental benefit.

LECTURER: Some cities have gone further and made green roofs compulsory. In one European city, for example, all new buildings with flat roofs must now include planting. Researchers are now studying whether this kind of policy actually lowers temperatures across a whole district, not just on individual buildings. The early results are encouraging, but more data will be needed before we can be certain.
LECTURER: Next week, we'll look at another approach: cool pavements.

passages.title: Cork: an ancient material with a modern future
paragraphs: Across the western Mediterranean, and particularly in the south of Portugal and Spain, extensive woodlands of cork oak have shaped both the landscape and the regional economy for centuries. The cork oak is unusual among commercially valuable trees because the part that is harvested is neither its timber nor its fruit but its outer bark, a thick and spongy layer that the tree regenerates after it has been stripped. Provided the work is carried out skilfully, the removal causes no lasting damage, and a single tree may continue to yield cork for well over two hundred years.

Human use of the material is remarkably old. Archaeologists have recovered cork floats attached to fishing nets in Mediterranean settlements dating back several thousand years, and classical writers described its use in footwear, beehives and the stoppers of storage jars. It was not until the seventeenth century, however, that cork acquired the role for which it is now best known. The spread of glass bottles strong enough to be laid on their side created a demand for a stopper that would remain tightly sealed for years, and cork proved ideally suited to that purpose.

The explanation for this suitability lies in the internal structure of the bark. Examined under a microscope, cork consists of millions of tiny, closely packed cells, each a sealed compartment containing a gas comparable in composition to air. Because these compartments make up most of its volume, the material is extraordinarily light, and it floats readily on water. The cell walls contain a waxy substance called suberin, which makes them almost impermeable to liquids and gases, while their flexible structure allows the material to be compressed and then to recover its original dimensions once the pressure is released.

The harvest itself remains a manual craft that machines have largely failed to replace. A tree cannot be stripped for the first time until it is about twenty-five years old, and the bark obtained from this initial harvest is irregular and too coarse for stoppers, so it is generally ground up for use in other products. Thereafter the bark is removed at intervals of approximately nine years, always during the summer months, when the tree is actively growing and the outer layer separates most cleanly. Workers use short-handled axes to cut and lift the bark in large curved sheets, a task demanding considerable experience, since a careless blow that reaches the living tissue beneath can permanently reduce the quality of future harvests.

Only from the third harvest onwards, when a tree is typically more than forty years old, is the bark of sufficient quality for the finest bottle stoppers. After stripping, the sheets are stacked outdoors for several months, then boiled in water, a process that cleans them, removes impurities and makes the material more flexible. Stoppers are then punched directly from the thickest sections, while the remaining material is broken into granules that can be bonded together to manufacture lower-grade stoppers and a wide variety of other goods.

During the late twentieth century, the industry encountered serious difficulties. A proportion of bottles sealed with natural cork were spoiled by a chemical compound that gave the wine an unpleasant, musty smell, and many producers began to adopt alternatives made of plastic or aluminium. For a period, commentators predicted that the cork oak forests themselves might be abandoned, as landowners would no longer have any financial incentive to maintain them. In response, manufacturers invested heavily in testing and improved processing methods, and the frequency of such contamination has since fallen considerably.

At the same time, new applications have broadened the market. Granulated cork is now incorporated into flooring, wall coverings and sports equipment, and its insulating properties have attracted the interest of architects seeking natural construction materials. Because cork resists the transmission of heat, sound and vibration, it has also been employed in specialised engineering contexts, including the thermal protection of spacecraft components. Manufacturers frequently emphasise that waste from stopper production is rarely discarded: virtually all of it is redirected into these secondary products.

Conservationists, for their part, value the cork forests for reasons that extend well beyond commerce. The open woodlands, known in Portugal as montado, support an unusually wide range of plant and animal species, among them several endangered birds of prey. Since harvesting does not require trees to be felled, the forests can be exploited economically while remaining largely intact. Some researchers argue that stripped trees absorb more carbon dioxide as they regenerate their bark, although the scale of this effect remains a matter of debate. What seems clear is that the long-term survival of these landscapes depends to a considerable extent on a continuing demand for the material they produce.

passages.title: Why teenagers sleep late
paragraphs: Parents have long complained that adolescents are reluctant to go to bed at a reasonable hour and almost impossible to wake in the morning. For much of the twentieth century this behaviour was attributed to poor discipline, excessive socialising or, more recently, the attractions of screens. Over the past three decades, however, a substantial body of research has suggested that the pattern is rooted primarily in biology, and that the conventional school timetable may be poorly matched to the physiological needs of the students it is intended to serve. The shift in interpretation matters, because explanations that locate the problem in individual character tend to produce very different remedies from those that locate it in the structure of the institutions surrounding young people.

Central to this argument is the body's internal clock, the mechanism that regulates when we feel alert and when we feel drowsy over a twenty-four-hour cycle. One of the signals the clock uses to prepare the body for sleep is melatonin, a hormone released by the brain as darkness falls. In a series of laboratory studies, the sleep researcher Helen Varga measured melatonin levels in volunteers of different ages and found that during adolescence its evening release occurs considerably later than in childhood, in some cases by as much as two hours. Teenagers who stay awake late, she concluded, are frequently not choosing to resist sleep; their bodies have simply not yet begun to produce it. Varga also observed that the delay was not confined to any particular culture or social group, a finding that strengthened her view that it reflects a developmental change common to the species rather than a product of modern lifestyles.

A second process compounds the effect. Throughout the waking day, a chemical pressure to sleep gradually accumulates in the brain, and it is this pressure that eventually makes sleep irresistible. The neuroscientist Daniel Okafor has shown that in adolescents this pressure intensifies at a noticeably slower rate than it does in younger children. As a result, a fourteen-year-old may feel wide awake at an hour when a ten-year-old would be struggling to keep his eyes open, even if both woke at the same time that morning. Okafor emphasises that neither process operates in isolation; it is the combination of a late hormonal signal and a slowly accumulating sleep pressure that makes an early bedtime so difficult for many adolescents to achieve.

Most teenagers are thought to require between eight and ten hours of sleep each night, yet many secondary schools begin their lessons before eight o'clock. Students who cannot fall asleep before eleven or midnight therefore routinely obtain only six or seven hours. The early start is seldom justified on educational grounds; it frequently reflects the scheduling of shared school transport, which is cheaper to operate when buses can serve primary and secondary schools in successive runs. Okafor describes the outcome as a mismatch imposed on an entire generation for reasons that have little to do with learning.

The consequences of persistent sleep loss appear to be considerable. Students who regularly sleep for less than eight hours tend to achieve lower grades, find it harder to concentrate and are more likely to report symptoms of depression. There is also evidence that drowsy teenage drivers are involved in a disproportionate number of road accidents in the early morning. The psychologist Sara Lindqvist argues that because these effects accumulate gradually, they are easily mistaken for laziness or lack of motivation rather than recognised as signs of chronic fatigue. Teachers responsible for early lessons frequently report that the first period of the day is the least productive, with many students appearing physically present but mentally absent.

These findings have encouraged a number of education authorities to experiment with later start times. In one American district studied by the education researcher Paul Whitcombe, moving the beginning of the school day from 7.15 to 8.40 resulted in students sleeping, on average, around an hour longer each night. Attendance improved, fewer students were observed falling asleep in class, and the rate of car accidents involving teenage drivers declined. Whitcombe acknowledges, however, that the improvement in examination results was smaller and less consistent than many advocates had anticipated. The district also recorded a modest decline in visits to the school nurse for complaints such as headaches, which researchers interpreted as a further indication of improved wellbeing.

Not everyone is convinced that timetables should be changed. Critics point out that later finishing times reduce the hours available for sport, part-time employment and family responsibilities, and that the costs of reorganising transport can be substantial. Lindqvist adds that the late-night use of phones and tablets intensifies a natural tendency rather than creating it, since their light suppresses melatonin still further; changing the timetable without addressing evening habits, she warns, may therefore produce only part of the expected benefit. Others question whether the evidence from a handful of districts can be generalised to schools operating under very different conditions, and call for larger trials before national policies are altered.

passages.title: In defence of boredom
paragraphs: Few states of mind are as universally disliked as boredom, and modern societies have devised an unprecedented range of technologies to ensure that it need never be endured for long. In one frequently cited experiment, a majority of participants who were asked to sit alone with their thoughts for fifteen minutes elected to administer a mild electric shock to themselves rather than remain unoccupied. Yet in recent years a number of psychologists and philosophers have begun to argue that boredom is not merely an unpleasant condition to be escaped, but one that may perform a valuable function. Their claims deserve serious consideration, even if, as I shall suggest, they are occasionally overstated by enthusiastic popularisers.

Any defence of boredom must begin by establishing what the experience actually involves. It is frequently confused with idleness, yet the two are quite distinct: a passenger waiting for a delayed train may be bored, but so may a student attending a lecture crammed with information. Most researchers now define boredom as the frustrated desire for satisfying engagement, the awareness that one would like to be absorbed in something meaningful combined with an inability to find it. Understood in this way, boredom functions as an internal signal that our present circumstances are failing to meet our needs, and, like hunger or physical discomfort, its unpleasantness is precisely what makes it effective, since it compels us to alter our behaviour. It should also be distinguished from apathy: whereas an apathetic individual is indifferent to whether he or she is engaged, a bored person cares intensely, which explains why boredom is experienced as restlessness rather than calm.

From this perspective, the difficulty with contemporary life is not that we are bored too often, but that we have become remarkably efficient at extinguishing the sensation before it has accomplished anything. When we reach for a device at the first flicker of restlessness, we satisfy the immediate craving for stimulation without considering whether our time might be better spent. The signal is silenced, but the underlying situation persists. I suspect that this goes some way towards explaining why so many people describe themselves as constantly occupied and yet persistently unfulfilled: our devices are superbly effective at supplying something to do, but considerably less effective at supplying something worth doing. Nor is the complaint entirely novel. Commentators in earlier generations voiced similar anxieties about newspapers, radio and television, and nineteenth-century philosophers worried about the corrosive effects of perpetual distraction. What has altered is not the temptation itself but the speed and convenience with which it can now be satisfied.

Some evidence also suggests that boredom may stimulate creative thinking. In a study conducted at a British university, volunteers who first spent a period performing a deliberately tedious task, copying telephone numbers from a directory, subsequently generated more original responses in a test of creative thinking than a comparison group who had not. The researchers proposed that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that this undirected mental activity permits unexpected associations to form. The effect was modest, however, and the experiment has not been replicated on a substantial scale, so it would be imprudent to build ambitious conclusions upon it. Nevertheless, its findings are consistent with the testimony of numerous writers and scientists who attribute their most productive insights to periods of apparent inactivity. It is also conceivable that the volunteers were simply more motivated by the creative task because it offered relief from what had preceded it, an alternative explanation the original researchers did not entirely exclude.

None of this implies that boredom is invariably beneficial. Chronic boredom, of the kind endured by individuals trapped in monotonous employment or deprived of meaningful opportunities, is associated with impaired health, reckless behaviour and depression. It would be both insensitive and absurd to inform someone in such circumstances that their condition is secretly a gift. The productive variety of boredom is brief and intermittent, and, crucially, it arises in situations where the individual possesses sufficient freedom to respond to it by changing course. Any account that celebrates boredom without acknowledging this distinction risks trivialising the experience of those for whom it is not a passing inconvenience but a persistent feature of daily existence.

What practical conclusions, then, might reasonably be drawn? Several educationalists have argued that children's lives have become so comprehensively scheduled that they seldom have the opportunity to experience boredom and to develop strategies for dealing with it independently. Instead of filling every afternoon with supervised activities, they recommend that parents deliberately leave some periods unstructured. I find this argument largely persuasive, although it can easily be pushed too far: a child abandoned for hours with nothing whatsoever to do is not necessarily cultivating imagination. The objective is not to manufacture boredom, but to refrain from rescuing children from it the moment it appears. Such advice, it should be noted, is easier to follow for families with flexible working hours and access to safe outdoor space, and its practicality may vary considerably from one household to another.

For adults, the implications are perhaps more straightforward. The next time you find yourself waiting with nothing to occupy you, it may be worth resisting the impulse to reach for your phone, if only for a few minutes, and to observe the thoughts that arise in the absence of external stimulation. The sensation that follows will probably be uncomfortable, and there is no guarantee that it will lead anywhere remarkable. But it may also prove to be the moment at which you recognise what you would genuinely prefer to be doing, which is, after all, precisely the information that boredom exists to provide.

task1.prompt: The diagram below shows how rainwater is collected and treated for use in homes. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

figure.title: Collecting and treating rainwater for household use
steps: Leaf filter removes leaves and debris
First-flush tank discards dirty initial water

branch.label: Overflow pipe to garden when tank is full

figure.alt: A nine-stage process: rain falls on a roof; gutters carry it to a downpipe; a leaf filter removes leaves and debris; a first-flush tank discards the dirty first water; the water is stored in an underground tank (with an overflow pipe to the garden when full); a pump sends it through a sand filter and then ultraviolet light, which kills bacteria; finally it reaches kitchen and bathroom taps.
figure.note: Illustrative diagram for practice; fictional system.

task1.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher discussion after the mock. Not a certified band answer.
task1.model:
The diagram illustrates the stages by which rainwater is collected from a roof and made safe for use in a home.

Overall, the process involves nine stages, which fall into two main phases: collection and storage, followed by treatment before the water reaches the taps. Water is cleaned three times along the way, and excess water is diverted to the garden.

In the first phase, rain falling on the roof is carried by gutters to a downpipe. It then passes through a leaf filter, which removes leaves and other debris. Because the first water to arrive is the dirtiest, it is discarded in a first-flush tank, and the remaining water is stored in an underground tank. When this tank is full, an overflow pipe takes the extra water to the garden.

In the second phase, a pump draws water from the storage tank and sends it through a sand filter. After this, ultraviolet light is used to kill bacteria. The treated water is finally supplied to taps in the kitchen and bathroom.
checklist: Task Achievement: Is there a clear overview of the main stages? Are all key stages covered accurately, in order?
Coherence and Cohesion: Are sequence markers used naturally (first, then, after this, finally)? Is the description logically paragraphed?
Lexical Resource: Are process words precise (carried, removed, discarded, diverted, treated)?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Is the passive used accurately? Are complex sentences controlled?

task2.prompt: Some people believe that every child should learn to play a musical instrument at school. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
task2.model_label: Illustrative model for teacher discussion after the mock. Not a certified band answer.
task2.model:
Music lessons are a familiar part of many school timetables, but whether every child should be required to learn an instrument is less clear. In my view, all children should be given the opportunity to learn one, although making it compulsory for everyone would not be the best use of limited school time.

There are strong arguments for giving every child access to instrumental lessons. Learning an instrument develops skills that are useful far beyond music, including concentration, patience and the ability to practise regularly. It can also be a powerful source of confidence, particularly for children who do not shine in academic subjects. Perhaps most importantly, instruments are expensive and private lessons are costly, so without school provision, only children from wealthier families would have the chance to discover a talent for music.

However, requiring every child to learn an instrument raises practical and educational problems. Schools already struggle to fit core subjects such as mathematics and languages into the week, and a compulsory instrument would take time away from these or from other creative subjects such as art and drama. Moreover, a child who has no interest in music is unlikely to benefit from being forced to practise, and may simply come to resent it. Learning an instrument well requires motivation, which compulsion rarely creates.

A better approach, therefore, would be for schools to offer every child a free introductory course, perhaps for a year in primary school, and then provide continued lessons for those who wish to carry on. This would remove the financial barrier while respecting children's different interests.

In conclusion, while I agree that every child should have the chance to learn an instrument at school, I do not believe it should be compulsory for all.
checklist: Task Response: Is a clear position stated and maintained? Are both the benefits and the limits of the idea addressed?
Coherence and Cohesion: Does each body paragraph have one central idea? Is referencing clear?
Lexical Resource: Is vocabulary on education and music precise and varied?
Grammatical Range and Accuracy: Is there a mix of simple and complex sentences, mostly error-free?
